title: 71% of India's Asian Games Medals Came From Just Five Sports
excerpt: Athletics, shooting, archery, boxing and wrestling produced 60 of India's 85 medals at Aichi-Nagoya 2026 — a concentration that keeps India fourth in Asia but raises questions about Olympic breadth.
body:
• Athletics (24 medals), shooting (15), archery (9), boxing (6) and wrestling (6) produced 60 of India's 85 medals at Aichi-Nagoya 2026 — 71% of the haul from just five sports.
  • India finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze — its second-best Asian Games total, behind only the record 106-medal campaign at Hangzhou 2023.
  • Efficiency improved: a leaner 495-athlete contingent (down from 661) lifted medals per 100 athletes from 16.0 to 17.2 — a 7.1% gain.
  • The Olympic test ahead: boxing's growth and golf's first women's individual gold point to where new medal streams must come from before Los Angeles 2028.

India's Asian Games campaign in Aichi-Nagoya ended with 85 medals and fourth place — the country's second-best haul in history. The headline number is worth celebrating. The shape of it deserves a harder look: 60 of those 85 medals came from just five sports. Athletics, shooting, archery, boxing and wrestling delivered 71 percent of India's total, leaving 16 other disciplines to split the rest.

Where the medals came from

Athletics was India's engine room with 24 medals, though only one of them gold — the women's 4x400m relay. Shooting contributed 15 medals including three golds, led by Neeru Dhanda's double gold in women's and mixed trap. Archery was the gold-medal leader with five, boxing added three golds through Lovlina Borgohain, Parveen Hooda and Ankush Panghal, and wrestling chipped in two golds via Sujeet Kalkal and Aman Sehrawat.

https://x.com/NewsArenaIndia/status/2107822998191579306

Beyond the big five, bright spots included a hockey double — the women's title ending a 44-year wait — defended golds for both cricket teams (the men beating Pakistan by 19 runs) and both kabaddi teams, India's first women's individual golf gold via Pranavi Urs, and breakout archer Kumkum Mohod's three medals including two golds.

The efficiency story underneath

The raw tally fell from the record 106 at Hangzhou 2023 to 85. But the contingent shrank faster — from 661 athletes to 495, a 25 percent cut. Measured per 100 athletes, India's medal rate actually improved from 16.0 to 17.2, a 7.1 percent efficiency gain. The declines were concentrated: shooting dropped seven medals, athletics five, rowing four. Boxing, notably, was the biggest improver with two additional medals.

Set against Asia's hierarchy, the question sharpens: China finished with 169 golds and 341 medals; Japan took 83 golds and 269; South Korea 39 golds and 150. Japan won roughly four golds for every one of India's; China won eight. One Indian sports analysis put it bluntly: the medal table reads less like a map of talent than a map of money, systems and sporting habit — and the real question is why some countries create an environment where becoming a good athlete is a realistic life choice, while in others it remains an enormous gamble.

"The medal table reads like a map of money, systems and sporting habit more than a map of talent."

— India Sports Hub, analysis of the Aichi-Nagoya campaign

Why concentration matters for LA 2028

A narrow medal base is a risk profile. When shooting has an off fortnight — down seven medals — or athletics converts only one gold from 24, little elsewhere absorbs the shortfall. At the Olympics the base narrows further: India has never won an Olympic medal in archery or badminton gold in athletics outside Neeraj Chopra's orbit, and sports like kabaddi and cricket's Asian dominance don't translate to the Olympic program in the same way.

Diversification must come from boxing's growth and Olympic pedigree, golf's breakthrough, and the small footholds in squash, badminton, weightlifting and table tennis — each needs systematic investment to become an Olympic podium. Indian boxers offered a parallel signal at the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games: 10 medals including seven gold, their best-ever haul.

A barometer the diaspora watches

For Indians abroad, the Asian Games are a two-week barometer of the country's rise, watched in living rooms from New Jersey to Sydney. The cricket and kabaddi golds, the hockey double and the women's 44-year wait ending are the moments that travel through diaspora WhatsApp groups and community screenings. That emotional connection is real, and it is also a reminder: the diaspora celebrates the wins, but the pipeline that produces them — coaching systems, sports science, school-level talent funnels — is still concentrated in a handful of disciplines and a handful of states.

What's next

Doha 2030 and, more urgently, Los Angeles 2028 are the next markers. India's task is twofold: protect the base — shooting and athletics must rebound — and deliberately widen it. If the 71 percent concentration narrows further toward a broader spread across eight or ten sports, the fourth-place finish in Asia starts looking like a platform rather than a ceiling. If it doesn't, India will keep celebrating strong Asian Games while the Olympic medal table tells a thinner story.
